characterList.description: A white man with short brown hair, a goatee and a mustache, dressed in a light-blue, orange and white plaid shirt over a grey T-shirt. He is wearing a wedding band on his left ring finger.
characterList.name: Dr. Long

content_metadata.description: A tutorial video presented by Dr. Long, illustrating the assembly and understanding of a cyclohexane model, focusing on its chair conformation and the ring flip process.

qAndA.answer: Dr. Long uses six tetrahedral carbons.
qAndA.question: What type of carbons are used to assemble the cyclohexane model?

qAndA.answer: The most stable conformation is the chair conformation.
qAndA.question: What is the most stable conformation of cyclohexane?

qAndA.answer: All axial hydrogens become equatorial, and all equatorial hydrogens become axial.
qAndA.question: What happens to the positions of hydrogen atoms during a ring flip?

qAndA.answer: The boat conformation is less stable due to the close proximity of certain hydrogen atoms, leading to steric strain.
qAndA.question: Why is the boat conformation less stable than the chair conformation?

scenes.contextualRelevance: The video is highly relevant to students and enthusiasts of organic chemistry, providing a clear, practical demonstration of cyclohexane's conformations.

narrativeProgression.description: Dr. Long introduces the video and its purpose: to demonstrate how to assemble a cyclohexane model and discuss its chair conformation.
Dr. Long assembles the model, explaining how to connect six tetrahedral carbons to create a hexane chain.
Dr. Long demonstrates how to fold the hexane chain into the chair conformation of cyclohexane.
Dr. Long explains and demonstrates the ring flip process in cyclohexane, highlighting the transition from axial to equatorial positions for hydrogen atoms.

scenes.title: Introduction and Molecular Model Assembly

climax.description: Dr. Long explains and demonstrates the ring flip process in cyclohexane.

content_metadata.title: Exploring Cyclohexane: Molecular Modeling and Chair Conformation

trimmingSuggestions.description: The initial introduction could be trimmed to start directly with the model assembly. This would make the video more engaging from the start.

text_to_speech: Hi. This is Dr. Long. This video is to look at your model kit and to put together cyclohexane and to talk a little bit about cyclohexane. I'm doing this from my iPhone just to show you how easy this is. What I've done is I've taken six tetrahedral carbons and I've put these all together in a row to essentially make hexane (linear) by itself. As you might see and as you've already been building and recording some of your isomer videos, you can tell that any alkanes that are singly bonded have free rotation. We talked in the collaborate session about looking at these from the Newman projection and talking about how we rotate and the energy conformations accordingly. So if you have six (carbons) placed in a row just take the end two and put them together and you may look and see that it is definitely not planar. There are all of these bends and wonkiness going on :). What we want to do is put our left hand on one carbon and put our right hand on the opposite carbon. We want to hold our left or hold our right hand in place, in this case I'm going to hold my left hand in place and I'm going to pull down this other carbon (opposite). The one in my left hand I'm going to pull up and I'm going to do so until it stops. So again, I'm going to walk you through that. It may already be in that conformation (chair) for you. So I'm going to pull one up and one down and what you're going to see is that it sort of looks like a lawn chair conformation and this is what we call the "chair" conformation. If you have it in the chair conformation and you sit it down on your desk, what you're going to see essentially is that you have three hydrogens facing down on the desk and you have three hydrogens that are sticking directly up. These are the axial hydrogens. And then we have around here, all the way what we call the equator or the equatorial positions we have the other six hydrogens. So we know we have C6H12 (formula). So we have six hydrogens in the axial positions, located up and down, so three up and three down. And then we have six hydrogens that are in equatorial positions all the way around. This is the most stable conformation of cyclohexane. So, if you have your model kit, I would like for you to go ahead and try and build the chair conformation and go ahead and look at that. Then we're going to walk it through through the boat conformation. So, I'm going to pull it up on one side into the half-chair and that's where the ring is flat and only one (carbon) is angled up. And I'm going to move right on up into the boat conformation and your going to see the proximity of these two hydrogens here are actually quite close to one another. And because of space and where these reside, this is a higher energy conformer. Cyclohexane does not like to exist in this conformation. Well, if we pull the other side down, what we've now done is essentially what we call a "ring flip". Now we're back to the original chair conformation but it's the opposite one. So I want you to see what happens when we go from one chair to the other (opposite) chair. Take note up here of this axial hydrogen. I'm going to move this one (carbon) up and this one (carbon) down. Notice now that this one goes into an equatorial position. So what we've discovered is that when we go from one chair conformation to the other chair conformation, all of the axial hydrogens become equatorial and all of the equatorial hydrogens become axial. We are not simply flipping this (ring) over. That's not what a ring flip is. A ring flip is when you walk through the conformations by simply moving the two end carbons (C1/C6) up and down accordingly. I hope this video was helpful to you and we will talk about this in our collaborate this week. Alright, thanks!
